appraisal_events.evidence: le sentiment qu'il éprouvait pour [Odette] n'étant plus mêlé de douleur, n'était plus guère de l'amour; des sentiments... rendraient Odette plus humaine (plus semblable aux autres femmes); quand Swann ramassa... la preuve que Forcheville avait été l'amant d'Odette, il s'aperçut qu'il n'en ressentait aucune douleur
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator traces the extinguishing of Swann's passion: Odette shifts from a uniquely idealized, painfully loved figure into an ordinary woman comparable to others, so much so that proof of her affair with Forcheville no longer wounds him.

appraisal_events.evidence: elle prenait congé de tout le monde... sans prendre à part Swann, sans lui dire où elle le reverrait le soir ou un autre jour; il éprouvait de la haine pour Odette, il aurait voulu crever ses yeux qu'il aimait tant tout à l'heure
appraisal_events.explanation: In Swann's dream, Odette leaves without singling him out or telling him when they will meet again, apparently favoring Forcheville (disguised as Napoléon III), and Swann's tenderness collapses into jealous hatred; since this occurs entirely within a self-generated dream, it is uncertain how much it reflects any real dynamic versus Swann's own residual anxiety.

status_effects.explanation: Odette loses her singular, painfully idealized place in Swann's heart, becoming 'plus semblable aux autres femmes' rather than uniquely beloved.
Swann is freed from the suffering that once defined his love, gaining calm and even indifference where he formerly felt anguish, as when he learns of Forcheville's affair with Odette without pain.
Within the dream, Swann is excluded from Odette's confidence and overtaken by jealous anguish and hatred, a stark reversal of his waking detachment.

ambiguities: The dream figure named 'Napoléon III' is explicitly identified by the narrator as actually representing Forcheville ('mais en réalité... c'était bien Forcheville'), not the historical Napoléon III; resolved as Forcheville here rather than left as a separate figure.

E2's snub occurs entirely within Swann's self-generated dream (the narrator notes Swann even splits his own identity into two dream figures), so its narrative_stance is left uncertain rather than endorsed as a real social event.
